author: beaver state news
title: Water concerns rise over major AI data center project in southern New Mexico
text:
Hopes for economic growth from a large artificial intelligence data center in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, are facing scrutiny as residents question how the facility will secure enough water amid ongoing drought conditions, according to a Jun. 17 report.
The 1,400-acre development, known as “Project Jupiter,” is being built near the Texas border and is described by NPR News as one of the largest data centers in the country. The site is linked to Oracle and OpenAI, with projections that full buildout could result in up to $165 billion in investment. Last year, county officials approved the project using industrial revenue bonds—a tax incentive often used for large developments.
Supporters of Project Jupiter say corporate projections include several hundred new jobs, $360 million allocated for schools and infrastructure, $50 million for the local water utility, and $12 million annually in county revenue. These community pledges are made instead of property tax payments by the tech companies involved—taxes that would otherwise total billions of dollars.
Despite these promised benefits, many residents and lawmakers remain concerned about unanswered questions regarding water use. They say approval was granted too quickly given uncertainty about resource consumption. Developers have stated that Project Jupiter will use water rights obtained from a nearby sod farm and claim overall consumption will stay below what that farm previously used; however, critics remain skeptical due to shifting estimates and changing project details over time.
The issue extends beyond this single development because regional water scarcity has intensified: The lower Rio Grande frequently runs dry during parts of the year; groundwater levels are falling; and New Mexico faces new interstate agreements requiring retirement of thousands of acres of irrigated farmland. Colin Cox, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, said, “Will that water even be there when Jupiter needs it or is it just water on paper?”
Project Jupiter also highlights growing connections between artificial intelligence expansion and electric grid demands. Data centers require significant power for operations and cooling systems—potentially straining grids further if fossil fuels are involved—and may affect utility costs or create security risks if oversight does not keep pace with rapid expansion.
